Water and weak interactions

Water and weak interactions

Hydrogen bonding, the properties of water, ice and density, ionisation and pH, and water transport in the xylem, all in one place. Biology cards are blue and orange; chemistry cards that explain the same ideas are pink and purple. Each topic ends with an IMAT trap check.

Biology cardChemistry cardIMAT trap check
1.1

The water molecule

Water, H₂O, has one oxygen atom joined to two hydrogen atoms by covalent bonds (shared pairs of electrons). Oxygen attracts the shared electrons more strongly than hydrogen does, so:

  • oxygen carries a partial negative charge (δ−);
  • each hydrogen carries a partial positive charge (δ+);
  • the molecule is bent (about 104.5°), so the two polar bonds do not cancel. The molecule is polar, with a net dipole, but overall it is electrically neutral.

Connects to: Every property in this module (cohesion, solvent action, high specific heat, ice structure) follows from this polarity.

Electronegativity is the ability of an atom to attract the shared electrons in a covalent bond. On the Pauling scale oxygen is 3.44 and hydrogen 2.20. The difference (1.24) makes each O–H bond polar covalent.

Oxygen has four regions of electrons: two bonding pairs and two lone pairs. They try to sit in a tetrahedral arrangement (109.5°), but lone pairs repel more strongly than bonding pairs and squeeze the H–O–H angle to 104.5°. A linear shape would have cancelled the dipoles; the bent shape is why water is polar.

Shape check: CO₂ also has polar bonds but is linear, so its dipoles cancel and the molecule is non-polar. Polar bonds do not guarantee a polar molecule.
1.2

Hydrogen bonds and weak interactions

A hydrogen bond is the attraction between a δ+ hydrogen (bonded to a very electronegative atom) on one molecule and a lone pair on a δ− oxygen of another.

  • Each water molecule can form up to four hydrogen bonds: two using its hydrogens and two using the lone pairs on its oxygen.
  • Each bond is weak (about 20 kJ/mol, around one twentieth of an O–H covalent bond), but there are so many that together they hold liquid water together.
  • In liquid water the bonds are constantly breaking and re-forming (about a trillion times a second), so water flows yet stays cohesive.

Connects to: Hydrogen bonds also hold DNA base pairs together (Module 6) and shape proteins (Module 5).

Inside a molecule, covalent bonds are strong. Between molecules (or between parts of large molecules) the forces are much weaker. Boiling water overcomes the weak forces and leaves the covalent bonds untouched.

InteractionWhereStrengthRole in living things
Covalent bondWithin moleculesStrongPeptide bonds, phosphodiester bonds
Hydrogen bondBetween δ+ H and N, O, F lone pairsWeak (≈ 20 kJ/mol)DNA base pairs, protein secondary structure, water cohesion
Hydrophobic interactionNon-polar groups pushed together by waterWeakProtein folding, membranes
Van der WaalsAll molecules, very short rangeVery weakEnzyme–substrate fit
Weak but useful: many weak bonds add up to a stable structure, and each can break and re-form. That reversibility lets DNA unzip and enzymes bind and release substrates.

Connects to: Proteins (Module 5), DNA (Module 6), lipid bilayers (Module 4).

Compare the hydrides of group 16. Going down from H₂S to H₂Te the boiling point rises as molecules get bigger (stronger London forces). If water followed the trend it would boil near −90 °C and be a gas at room temperature. In reality it boils at 100 °C, about 190 °C higher, because of hydrogen bonding.

FON rule: hydrogen bonds need H bonded to F, O or N. S–H is not polar enough, so H₂S has no significant hydrogen bonding.
1.3

Cohesion, adhesion and surface tension

Cohesion is the attraction between molecules of the same substance. For water it is due to hydrogen bonds.

Surface tension arises because a molecule at the surface has no neighbours above it. It is pulled inwards and sideways by cohesion, so the surface acts like a stretched skin. This lets small insects walk on water and makes drops round. Water's surface tension is high (≈ 72 mN/m at 20 °C) compared with most liquids because of its hydrogen bonding.

Adhesion is the attraction between different substances, for example water hydrogen-bonding to the –OH groups of cellulose or glass.

When adhesion to the wall is stronger than cohesion, water climbs the wall and the surface curves upwards into a concave meniscus. In a narrow tube this lifts the whole column: capillary action. The narrower the tube, the higher the water rises.

Simulation: capillary rise


Clean glass, water at 20 °C, contact angle taken as 0°: h = 2γ / (ρgr) ≈ 14.9 mm² / r. The shaded band marks typical xylem vessel radii (about 10–100 µm). You do not need the formula for IMAT.

Connects to: Water movement in xylem (deck 1.8) relies on both properties.

1.4

Water as a solvent

Water dissolves many substances because its partial charges attract ions and other polar molecules. Water molecules cluster around each solute particle, forming a hydration shell that keeps the particles apart.

  • Hydrophilic substances (ions, polar molecules such as glucose, amino acids, ethanol) dissolve.
  • Hydrophobic substances (non-polar, such as hydrocarbons and fats) do not dissolve. Water molecules prefer bonding to each other, so non-polar molecules are pushed together.

Connects to: Hydrophobic clustering drives lipid bilayers (Module 4) and the folding of proteins (Module 5).

A solute dissolves when the new attractions to the solvent (ion–dipole or hydrogen bonds) make up for the attractions that must be broken in the solute and in the solvent.

Type of substanceExampleIn water
IonicNaClDissolves (ion–dipole attractions)
Polar covalent, can hydrogen-bondGlucose, ethanol, NH₃Dissolves (hydrogen bonds)
Non-polarHexane, fats, oilsDoes not dissolve
Also in cells: water is the medium for transport (blood plasma, sap) and reactions, and it takes part in them: it is split in hydrolysis and released in condensation.
1.5

Heat, latent heat and phase change

Specific heat capacity (c) is the energy needed to raise 1 g of a substance by 1 °C. Latent heat (L) is the energy absorbed or released when 1 g changes state without a change in temperature. Energy supplied to a state change goes into potential energy (loosening intermolecular attractions), not kinetic energy, so temperature does not rise.

QuantityValue for waterUse
c (liquid)4.18 J g⁻¹ °C⁻¹Q = m c ΔT
c (ice)≈ 2.09 J g⁻¹ °C⁻¹Q = m c ΔT
c (steam)≈ 2.0 J g⁻¹ °C⁻¹Q = m c ΔT
L fusion (melting)334 J g⁻¹Q = m L
L vaporisation (boiling)2260 J g⁻¹Q = m L

Water's specific heat is unusually high because added energy first goes into stretching and breaking hydrogen bonds instead of making molecules move faster. Boiling needs about 6.8 times more energy than melting (2260 ÷ 334) because nearly all the remaining hydrogen bonds must be broken.

Add heat to 1 g of ice at −20 °C


Conceptual 2D model. Dashed orange lines are hydrogen bonds. Real liquid water keeps most of its hydrogen bonds until boiling; the numbers shown are illustrative.

StageWorkingEnergy
Warm ice to 0 °C10 × 2.09 × 10209 J
Melt ice10 × 3343 340 J

Boil water10 × 226022 600 J

Total≈ 30 500 J (30.5 kJ)
Trap: the temperature stays constant during melting and boiling, so use Q = mL for those stages, not Q = mcΔT. Boiling is by far the largest term.
  • Temperature stability: water's high specific heat means large amounts of heat cause small temperature changes, protecting cells, bodies and aquatic habitats (and moderating climates near the sea).
  • Evaporative cooling: the fastest molecules escape as vapour, taking 2260 J per gram with them. Sweating and transpiration use this to cool the body or leaf.
  • Aquatic life: ponds and oceans change temperature slowly, so organisms live in a stable environment.
1.6

Ice, density and the phase diagram

In ice every water molecule forms four hydrogen bonds in a tetrahedral arrangement with its neighbours (O···O ≈ 0.28 nm). This builds an open hexagonal lattice with empty space inside the rings. When ice melts a modest fraction of the hydrogen bonds break (about 15% is a common estimate), the cage collapses and molecules move closer together. That is why ice is less dense than liquid water.

Simulation: the ice cage


circle = oxygen of a water moleculedashed line = hydrogen bond (the H lies on the line)

Oxygen positions follow the real hexagonal ice (Ih) lattice. Drag to rotate. Press “Look down the channels” to see the hexagonal rings; slide “Melt it” to watch order and volume change.

Density = mass ÷ volume. Ice (0.917 g/cm³) is less dense than liquid water (≈ 1.000 g/cm³ at 4 °C), so it floats with about 92% of its volume below the surface. Water expands by about 9% on freezing, which is why frozen pipes burst.

Liquid water is densest at about 4 °C. Warming from 0 to 4 °C, fragments of ice-like structure collapse and the density rises; above 4 °C ordinary thermal expansion wins and the density falls.

Simulation: density against temperature


In autumn the surface water cools, becomes denser and sinks. This continues until all the water is at about 4 °C. Further cooling makes surface water less dense, so it stays on top and freezes. The ice layer floats and insulates the water below, which stays liquid (around 4 °C at the bottom) so aquatic life survives the winter. If ice sank, lakes would freeze from the bottom up.

A phase diagram shows which state is stable at each temperature and pressure. Lines mark where two states coexist.

  • Triple point: the single temperature and pressure where solid, liquid and gas coexist in equilibrium: 0.01 °C (273.16 K) and 0.006 atm (611.7 Pa).
  • Critical point: above 374 °C and 218 atm liquid and gas cannot be told apart (supercritical fluid).
  • Sublimation: below the triple-point pressure, ice turns straight to vapour (used in freeze-drying).
  • Unusual slope: the solid–liquid line of water leans to the left: raising the pressure lowers the melting point slightly, because ice is less dense than water.
  • Boiling point depends on pressure: water boils when its vapour pressure equals the external pressure.

Simulation: boiling point against pressure


Connects to: Autoclaves sterilise instruments at about 121 °C, a temperature water can only reach as a liquid under raised pressure.

1.7

Ionisation of water and pH

Water is slightly ionised. Occasionally a proton (H⁺) moves along a hydrogen bond from one molecule to its neighbour:

2 H₂O ⇌ H₃O⁺ + OH⁻

The ions are hydronium (H₃O⁺), often written simply H⁺, and hydroxide (OH⁻). The equilibrium lies far to the left: in pure water at 25 °C only about one molecule in 550 million is ionised, so [H⁺] = [OH⁻] = 1 × 10⁻⁷ mol/dm³. Water can act as both an acid and a base (it is amphoteric).

  • Ionic product of water: Kw = [H⁺][OH⁻] = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ mol²/dm⁶ at 25 °C.
  • pH = −log₁₀[H⁺]. Pure water at 25 °C: pH = 7 (neutral). Acidic: pH below 7. Alkaline: above 7.
  • pH is logarithmic: each unit is a tenfold change in [H⁺]. At 25 °C, pH + pOH = 14.
  • Kw rises with temperature, so the pH of pure water falls (≈ 6.1 at 100 °C) but it is still neutral because [H⁺] = [OH⁻].

Move along the pH scale (25 °C)


Does temperature change “neutral”?

  • Blood is kept at pH 7.35–7.45 (slightly alkaline compared with neutral). At body temperature (37 °C) neutral pH is about 6.8.
  • Stomach contents are strongly acidic (about pH 2), which suits the enzyme pepsin. Small-intestine enzymes work best at around pH 7–8.
  • Enzymes have an optimum pH. Extremes change the charges on R groups, break ionic and hydrogen bonds, and denature the protein.
  • Buffers (for example the carbonic acid–hydrogen carbonate system in blood) resist changes in pH.

Connects to: Protein structure and denaturation (Module 5); enzymes and digestion.

1.8

Water transport in plants (xylem)

Plants take up a large amount of water and lose most of it (well over 90%) as vapour. The route is:

  1. Root hairs absorb water by osmosis
  2. Water crosses the cortex to the xylem (Casparian strip at the endodermis)
  3. Water rises through the xylem (cohesion–tension)
  4. Water evaporates from mesophyll cell walls into air spaces
  5. Water vapour diffuses out through stomata (transpiration)
Water potential (Ψ) is the tendency of water to move, measured in kPa or MPa. Pure water at atmospheric pressure is 0; solutes lower it (more negative). Water moves from higher (less negative) to lower (more negative) water potential. Soil → root → stem → leaf → air is a falling gradient.
  • Vessel elements (wide, joined end to end with open perforations) and tracheids (narrow, tapered, with pits) carry water and minerals upwards.
  • At maturity the cells are dead and hollow: no cytoplasm or end walls to slow flow, and no energy is needed from the xylem cells.
  • Walls are thickened with lignin (rings, spirals or networks) which makes them strong and waterproof, so they do not collapse under the tension.
  • Pits are thin areas where water can pass sideways between vessels.
  1. Transpiration: water evaporates from mesophyll cell walls and diffuses out of the leaf through open stomata.
  2. Evaporation lowers the leaf's water potential, pulling water out of the xylem: this creates tension (negative pressure).
  3. Cohesion (hydrogen bonds between water molecules) passes the pull down the unbroken column as a mass flow.
  4. Adhesion to the lignified walls supports the column and resists gravity.
  5. Water enters the roots to replace it (the transpiration stream).

Root pressure (from active ion uptake) adds a small push, mostly at night, but cannot explain water reaching the top of tall trees. Capillary action alone could lift water only a metre or so in xylem-sized tubes.

Factors that increase transpiration: more light (stomata open), higher temperature, lower humidity, more wind.

Illustrative water potentials (MPa): moist soil ≈ −0.3, root ≈ −0.6, stem ≈ −0.8, leaf ≈ −1.5, air at 50% humidity ≈ −95.

Connects to: Water-potential gradients also drive osmosis in cells.

Conceptual model. Beads are water molecules; dashed links are hydrogen bonds (cohesion). An air bubble breaks the chain in that vessel, so water bypasses it through pits into neighbouring vessels.

The pressure in a transpiring xylem vessel can be negative: water is being pulled, not pushed. Normally water at such low pressure would boil (see the phase diagram), but in narrow, clean, wettable xylem vessels there are no nucleation sites, so the liquid stays intact in a metastable state held together by hydrogen bonds. If an air bubble appears (cavitation), the column breaks, forming an embolism, and the vessel stops conducting.

1.9

Key terms deck

1.10

Trap recap

  • Boiling and melting break hydrogen bonds, not covalent bonds.
  • Polar bonds do not always mean a polar molecule: shape matters.
  • A water molecule makes up to four hydrogen bonds.
  • Orientation in solution: O faces cations, H faces anions.
  • Temperature is constant during a change of state; use Q = mL there and Q = mcΔT elsewhere.
  • Ice floats and water is densest at 4 °C, not 0 °C.
  • Pure water is neutral whenever [H⁺] = [OH⁻], even if its pH is not 7.
  • pH is logarithmic: 2 units = 100-fold.
  • The xylem is dead tissue: water rises by transpiration pull and cohesion, not by pumping.
